teaching.causalExplanation: Buying on terms means paying a deposit, a first payment up front, and then the same repayment at regular times until it's paid off. You take the TV home after the deposit. Here, the deposit is twenty per cent of sixteen hundred, three hundred and twenty dollars. Then come the repayments, eighteen of them, at seventy-eight dollars each. That's fourteen hundred and four dollars. So the total cost is the deposit plus all the repayments, seventeen hundred and twenty-four dollars. Count repayments carefully. Two years of monthly repayments is twenty-four, and three years of fortnightly repayments is seventy-eight. And don't add the deposit on top of the cash price. The deposit is part of what you pay, not something extra. So how much extra does terms cost? Take the cash price away from the total. Seventeen twenty-four minus sixteen hundred is a hundred and twenty-four dollars extra. Whatever the seller calls it, the extra is built into the repayments, so the only way to see it is to add everything up. Why would anyone pay more? Because you take the TV home after paying only three hundred and twenty dollars, and the seller waits for the rest. The extra is the price of that wait. As a percentage, measure it on the cash price, the price you'd pay today. A hundred and twenty-four divided by sixteen hundred is seven point seven five per cent. Dividing by the total, seventeen twenty-four, gives about seven point two per cent, which makes the deal look better than it is. Now total all four the same way. Every dollar that leaves your hand counts. Cash is sixteen hundred. Lay-by is sixteen hundred, plus an example ten-dollar fee, sixteen hundred and ten. Buy now, pay later is eight fortnightly payments of two hundred, plus an eight-dollar account fee for each of the four months, sixteen hundred and thirty-two. Terms is seventeen twenty-four. Lay-by costs almost nothing extra, but you wait for the TV. Put them in order. Notice the smallest repayment, seventy-eight dollars, sits on the biggest total. A small repayment, repeated many times, can cost the most. So compare totals, never repayments. Terms costs ninety-two dollars more than buy now, pay later, for exactly the same TV.

Buy now, pay later is eight fortnightly payments of two hundred, plus an eight-dollar account fee for each of the four months, sixteen hundred and thirty-two. Terms is seventeen twenty-four. Lay-by costs almost nothing extra, but you wait for the TV. Put them in order. Notice the smallest repayment, seventy-eight dollars, sits on the biggest total. A small repayment, repeated many times, can cost the most. So compare totals, never repayments. Terms costs ninety-two dollars more than buy now, pay later, for exactly the same TV.

scenes.teachingReason: But cheapest isn't automatically best. The best method depends on the buyer, so ask three questions. Can you pay cash now? Can you meet every repayment? And how urgent is it? Buyer one has seventeen hundred dollars saved. Cash is available, and it's a hundred and twenty-four dollars cheaper than terms, so cash suits her. Buyer two has two hundred dollars, and can put aside two hundred a fortnight. The old TV still works, so it isn't urgent. Lay-by suits him. He pays two hundred today and two hundred a fortnight after that, collects the TV in about three months, and pays just ten dollars extra, instead of a hundred and twenty-four on terms. And if a buyer can't meet every repayment on any plan, the honest answer is to wait and save first. A good answer names the buyer's situation, and quotes the numbers.
